It's 21 March, 7.15 p.m., at the Konzerthaus. Mrs Hoffmann is sitting in the dressing room in her navy-blue dress. Mara is with her. The concert starts in a quarter of an hour.
Mara, I can't. I'm going home. My hands are shaking.
Your hands are shaking because you're nervous. That's normal. It's called stage fright.
I know what stage fright is, child. I had it before every concert, for seventy years. But back then I was young. Although I was afraid, I knew my fingers worked.
Your fingers work. I've heard you every evening for three months. You practised every day, even though your back hurt.
And what if I forget a note? What if I stop in the middle of the piece?
Then you just keep playing anyway. Nobody in the hall is coming to hear a perfect pianist, but to hear you.
Who's out there? Probably just a few old people who feel sorry for me.
The hall is sold out. Two hundred seats. In the front row are Ludwig, Lena, the Nowak family with Kuba and Ola, and Mr Bauer's mother, Ilse, your former pupil. She's brought flowers.
Ilse? Little Ilse with the pigtails? She could never play scales properly, but she had a wonderful feeling for music.
She's seventy-five now. And she said that today she's coming not as a doctor, but as your pupil.
All right, then. I'm still afraid. Nevertheless, I'm going. Give me your hand, child. As far as the stage. I'll do the rest myself.
“op-VOHL”: stress on “wohl”, final b sounds like p.
“obwohl” introduces a subordinate clause (verb at the END). It expresses a contrast: something happens in spite of an obstacle.
She played, although she was afraid.
Although she was afraid, she played. (subordinate clause in position 1 → main verb straight after the comma)
He goes for a walk, although it's raining.
“trotzdem” is an adverb. It links two MAIN clauses. When it's in position 1, the verb comes straight after it (inversion):
It's raining, but he still goes for a walk.
She was afraid, but she played anyway. (trotzdem in the middle)
The relationship is the same as between “weil” and “deshalb”: “weil” (verb at the end) shows the cause, “deshalb” (position 1, verb in 2) shows the effect.
Both express contrast, but “sondern” (= but rather) is only used after a NEGATIVE, when you correct something:
She's old, but she plays well.
She's not coming as a doctor, but as a pupil.
The construction “nicht nur …, sondern auch …” = not only…, but also…: “Sie spielt nicht nur Chopin, sondern auch Bach.”

weil, obwohl, dass, wenn, als, ob
Memory trick: “ADUSO” = aber, denn, und, sondern, oder: these DON'T change the word order.
She's old, but she plays wonderfully.
It's raining, but I'm still going for a walk.

The Small Hall of the Konzerthaus was full. Two hundred people sat on red velvet seats under a white ceiling with gold ornaments. The first part of the evening belonged to the young musicians: a nineteen-year-old violinist, a cellist with blue hair, a clarinettist so nervous that he dropped his sheet music twice. Nevertheless, they all played wonderfully, and the audience applauded for a long time.

In the front row sat Kastanienallee. Ludwig was wearing a suit for the second time this year, a grey one this time, as he had given the blue one to Jonas. Lena was holding her phone, because Andrei wanted to watch on video from Sibiu. Kuba and Ola sat as still as two little statues, even though they otherwise never sat still. Next to them sat an elderly lady with white hair and a big bunch of white roses on her lap. Ilse.

Then the lights in the hall went down; only the stage stayed lit. In the middle stood a black piano. An old Steinway, the same one as in 1956. Mr Bauer had confirmed it to Mara on the phone, with a joy you could hear: “It's a little tired, like all of us. But it still plays.”

Ladies and gentlemen. Seventy years ago, in 1956, a young twenty-year-old pianist gave her first concert in this building. Her father sat in the front row, in his only suit. Tonight she has come back. Please join me in welcoming: Margarete Hoffmann.

She walked slowly onto the stage, on Mara's arm, in her navy-blue dress, with small, careful steps. Although her back was bent, she held her head high. At the piano she let go of Mara's arm. Mara went back into the wings. Mrs Hoffmann stood alone in front of two hundred people. She bowed once, deeply and elegantly, as a young woman had learned seventy years ago. Then she sat down.

For a long time she did nothing. She sat there, her hands in her lap, looking at the keys. The hall was so quiet that you could hear the old clock ticking in the foyer. Mara, behind the curtain, held her breath. Ludwig, in the front row, reached for Lena's hand.

Then she raised her hands and began. Chopin, the Nocturne in E-flat major. The first notes were slow and a little unsure. On the fifth note a finger trembled, and one note came too late. Mara closed her eyes. But Mrs Hoffmann played on. Nevertheless. And then, after a minute, something happened. Her hands grew calmer. Her back straightened. The music grew bigger, warmer, surer. It was as if the old woman at the piano grew a few years younger with every bar.

She played three pieces. After the second nobody applauded, because nobody wanted to break the spell. After the third, when the last note had faded away in the hall, there were ten seconds of complete silence. Then Ilse stood up. Then Ludwig. Then the whole front row. And then the whole hall, two hundred people applauding and applauding and not wanting to stop.

Mrs Hoffmann stood up, held on to the piano with one hand and bowed. Once. Twice. The third time, Mara saw that she was crying. Ilse went up to the stage and gave her the white roses. The two old women held hands for a long time, the teacher and the pupil, and said something to each other that nobody heard.

Mrs Hoffmann looked down at him and shook her head, as if to say: you old rascal. Then she sat down once more. She didn't play Chopin again, but an old, simple song. A children's song. “Guter Mond, du gehst so stille” (“Good moon, you go so quietly”). The song she had sung in the cellar during the war, for Mr Lewin, who was always crying. Many of the old people in the hall quietly sang along. Ludwig sang the loudest. And out of tune, as always.

After the concert the young musicians came to the dressing room, one after another, a little shy. The nineteen-year-old violinist asked how you overcome stage fright. Mrs Hoffmann looked at her for a long time and said: “You don't, my child. You don't overcome it. You play anyway. For seventy years. That's the whole secret.” The cellist with blue hair wanted to take a photo with her, and she insisted that Fritz be in the picture too, even though dogs were actually not allowed in the Konzerthaus. Mr Bauer pretended he hadn't seen anything. On Lena's phone, Andrei was waving from Sibiu and shouting in German: “Bravo, Frau Hoffmann! Bravo!” His mother stood behind him and applauded too, even though she didn't understand a word.

Later, in the dressing room, Mrs Hoffmann sat in front of the mirror, surrounded by flowers, drinking a glass of champagne, even though the doctor had forbidden it. Mara sat beside her, holding her hand. The old fingers were warm.
You know, child, today I played a wrong note. On the fifth note. Did you hear?
Yes. And still, it was the most beautiful concert I've ever heard.

Mrs Hoffmann smiled. “My father said the same thing back then. After my first concert. That time too I played a wrong note, on the seventh. He said: a wrong note shows that a human being is playing and not a machine. He was a wise man.” She took a sip of champagne and looked in the mirror at the old woman with white hair and shining eyes. “Seventy years,” she said quietly. “And it was just as beautiful as the first time. Thank you, Mara.”
Outside, by the dressing-room door, Ludwig was waiting with Fritz and a second glass of champagne. For himself, he said. But he gave it to her.
